title: Who is poor
hookLine: the poor person isn't the one with too little but the one who craves more

cards: Ask a friend how much money would make them feel secure, and remember the number. Ask again five years and two raises later. Quite often the number has moved, and it's still a little more than they have.
The target walks away as they walk toward it. Seneca wouldn't have been surprised.
At the end of his second letter, after telling Lucilius to stay with a few good authors, he hands him a thought he picked up that day, then gives it a twist that sticks.

teach.b: Seneca says he's been reading Epicurus, founder of a rival school, and found this: contented poverty is an honorable thing. Seneca likes it, then pushes it a step further.
If it's contented, it isn't really poverty at all. Then his own line. The poor person isn't the one who has too little.

teach.h: POOR IS THE ONE WHO CRAVES MORE.
teach.b: It's the one who craves more.

What does it matter, he asks, how much someone has locked in the safe or stored in the barn, how many flocks or how much interest, if they're always eyeing what belongs to someone else and counting what they don't have yet?
So what's the right measure of wealth?
First, Seneca says, to have what is necessary. Then, to have what is enough. Not a fixed number.
A line you draw yourself. One honest note: Seneca wrote this as a very rich man, and Tacitus records a critic in Seneca's own lifetime attacking him for that wealth. We'll come back to that gap.
But the idea doesn't depend on the man.

Look at the week we've walked: peace of mind, the pond unstirred; attention; thank you, teacher, at the Discourses' close; then Seneca's letters: dear friend, hold this hour, go deep, and now crave less.
Different days, one thread. Whoever keeps counting what they don't have yet is poor, whatever is in the safe.

how: Some people who practice Stoicism ask whether a desire is necessary or merely more, and set their own limit of enough instead of chasing a moving target.

games.q: you're Seneca, and you've just read Epicurus: contented poverty is an honorable thing. what do you add?
o: nothing: it's perfect as it is.
if it's contented, it isn't poverty at all.
games.why: Seneca pushes it further: contentment cancels poverty. the poor one is the one who craves more.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you've been wanting, new shoes, a bigger place, a little more in the account, and ask Seneca's two questions: is it necessary, and if not, do I already have enough without it?
Don't force an answer; let the want soften a little, like a balloon letting out some air, and notice what's already here that's enough for this minute.

wordCard.voice: Epicurus. The rival philosopher Seneca was reading: his line that contented poverty is honorable, which Seneca pushes further, since the poor person is the one who craves more.

orig.s: non qui parum habet, sed qui plus cupit, pauper est

orig.note: Latin: not the one who has too little, but the one who craves more, is poor.

carryVoice: Your line: crave less. First what's necessary, then what's enough. A week walked; see you tomorrow.
